title.en: Rolling without slip versus sliding friction

summary: Treat no-slip rolling as a kinematic constraint with static friction, and sliding as a separate kinetic-friction regime; do not infer either from a shiny material.
objective: On a stationary support, show zero instantaneous contact velocity for signed no-slip rolling and nonzero tangential contact velocity for sliding.
applies_when: A wheel, cylinder, ball or similar rigid body moves on a support and the viewer is asked to distinguish roll from slide.
An incline race or vehicle tyre is used to talk about friction and rotation together.
intent_signals: roll a barrel down a ramp without sliding
show the tyre patch at rest
why does the hollow cylinder slip
example_prompts: Race a sliding block against a rolling cylinder on the same incline and label which uses static friction.
Mark the contact point on a wheel and show when it is instantaneously at rest.
negative_signals: Decorative spinning wheels whose rotation is unrelated to travel.
Material roughness maps used as a friction coefficient.
not_for: Authored locomotion that only locks a foot visually.
Claims that optical roughness establishes traction.

principles: Rolling without slip constrains the instantaneous contact velocity relative to the support. A painted rim marker is momentarily stationary at contact, not fixed there throughout rotation.
Use signed rolling velocity and spin about a declared axis on a stationary plane; matching unsigned speed magnitudes alone does not establish no slip.
Static friction can sustain the constraint only within its available bound. Imposed rolling animation is a kinematic model, separate from a friction solver.
implementation: Own center position, signed tangential velocity, angular position/velocity, finite m,R,I>0, support frame and friction parameters. The general contact residual is v_CM + omega cross r_contact - v_surface.

For an undriven body already rolling or released from rest down a stationary incline under gravity, use a=g sin(theta)/(1+I/(m R²)), f_required=I a/R² and N=m g cos(theta). Require 0<=theta<pi/2 and f_required<=mu_s N before enforcing the signed v=R omega constraint.

If the static bound fails, evolve translation and spin separately with a declared kinetic-friction law opposing tangential slip; detect zero slip and recheck static feasibility. Do not carry the no-slip acceleration into this branch or into motor-driven motion.
Render the contact marker and signed residual from the same state. Pause preserves state; reset restores center pose, spin, linear/angular velocity and friction settings.
observable_checks: In the stationary-plane no-slip branch, the signed residual is zero within tolerance; reversing spin alone makes it nonzero.
The material point at contact is instantaneously at rest, then moves away as the body rotates.
When the static inequality fails, the model reports slipping rather than continuing to impose v=R omega. Visual roughness alone changes no friction state.

creative_affordances: Tyre squash, dust or skid marks can communicate slip without becoming the friction law.
Cutaway spokes or a ground grid make the contact-point rest condition readable.
known_limits: OpenStax rolling without slipping assumes a rigid symmetric body on a rigid surface; rolling resistance and deformation are out of scope.
Engine friction combine rules are implementation-defined and were not verified here.
Authored reusable guidance; no runtime artifact has been observed for this record.

claims.statement: For planar rolling on a stationary surface with the consistent signed roll convention, no slip means zero instantaneous contact velocity and v_CM=R omega. Static friction may act within its bound; sliding requires a separate tangential slip/friction model.
claims.scope: Rigid symmetric body on a stationary rigid plane, with declared spin sign; the gravity-only incline example excludes external driving torques, rolling resistance and tire deformation.

source_refs.locator: 11.1, Rolling without Slipping; Figure11.5, static-friction inequality and Eq11.4
